title: Bidirectional Dijkstra on New York (SoHo) ⚡
description: Visualizing Bidirectional Dijkstra pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡ Imagine shortest-path search that fans out from START and END at the same time—then stops when the waves meet. In this Amsterdam map simulation, we run two priority queues (forward + backward), keep best-known distances from each side, and continually update a shared “best path” bound when frontiers connect. Key intuition: Dijkstra’s correctness stays, but the explored area shrinks dramatically—often turning a painful full-map sweep into a tight corridor.

Takeaway: when you can define a target (or reverse edges), bidirectional search can cut work while preserving optimality.

Debate: should route engines always use bidirectional Dijkstra, or do heuristics (A*, ALT, contraction hierarchies) usually win in production?

fb_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra is a graph search method for shortest paths that expands from both the start and the destination until the search frontiers meet—often reducing explored nodes versus a single-ended run. In our Amsterdam visualization, you can literally see the two waves converge and tighten the best-path bound as edges relax.
